title: Memory bottlenecks, the organization of large HPC systems and the Grace Hopper superchip
transcript_provenance: Local machine transcription (faster-whisper small.en); not publisher captions
source_uncertainties: Wulf and McKee (1995), ACM SIGARCH Computer Architecture News 23(1) 20-24: the paper could not be downloaded (the ACM, ResearchGate and course-page copies returned 403 or 404 and the University of Virginia repository returned an empty response on 2026-10-26). Bibliographic data checked in Crossref (volume 23, issue 1, pages 20-24). The argument is cited as reported by Machanick (2002), Sec. 1, and criticised by Ertl (undated web page); the 50 % and 7 % per year growth rates are Machanick's, and he attributes the 7 % DRAM figure to the literature; this chapter did not trace them to the original.

Williams, Waterman and Patterson: the chapter read the Berkeley technical report UCB/EECS-2008-134 (October 2008). The published CACM article 52(4) (2009) was not opened; page numbers of the CACM article are not given.

Intel ARK page for the i5-12450H returned HTTP 403 to this chapter's scripted requests; Chapter 7 opened it on 2026-10-26 through a fetch agent. The maximum turbo frequency of 4.40 GHz is taken from Chapter 11's record. The 16 double-precision flop per cycle of a performance core (two 256-bit FMA pipes) was not checked in an Intel manual; the measured 66.7 Gflop/s on one thread is 95 % of 4.40 GHz x 16.

Kim et al. (ISCA 2008): the University of Maryland copy of the paper was read; it was not compared with the ACM version. The exact lower bound on channels per group pair in non-maximum dragonflies is garbled in the text extraction and is not quoted.

Frontier numbers: the lecture's slides (ORNL, 2024 data) agree with TOP500 for June 2024 (8 699 904 cores, 22 786 kW, Rpeak 1 714.81 Pflop/s, Rmax 1 206.00 Pflop/s). The OLCF user guide (retrieved 2026-10-26) gives 77 cabinets and 9 856 nodes and 23.9 Tflop/s per GCD; the HPE talk of February 2023 gives 9 408 nodes in 74 cabinets and 26.5 Tflop/s per GCD. The three peak values (2.014, 1.818 and 1.715 Eflop/s) are not reconciled. The HPE slide says up to 16 global links per switch (at most 512 per group, 7.0 per other group) and also '4 links between each of the 74 compute groups' (292 of the 512 ports; the two statements are compatible); the slide does not say where the other 220 global ports of a group go; support and storage groups are separate. The lecture's 74 groups x 128 nodes = 9 472 differs from 9 408 nodes; not resolved. The HPCG value of 14 054.0 Tflop/s is first listed on the HPCG list of November 2022 and unchanged to June 2026; compared with the Rpeak and Rmax of November 2022; the HPCG specification was not opened.

The 2025 GH200 datasheet table has two-line cells for the LPDDR5X size (480 GB; 120 GB, 240 GB) and bandwidth (up to 384 GB/s; up to 512 GB/s); the chapter reads them line by line (480 GB with 384 GB/s). The whitepaper (v1.21) says 'up to 500 GB/s'. The slide's 70 Tflop/s FP64 is not explained by the datasheet (34 vector, 67 tensor core). The 7x of thread-block clusters (slide) was not checked against the H100 whitepaper, which was not opened.

Energy values (35, 6.5, 5, 1.3 pJ per bit; 99, 62, 12 pJ per flop) are the values of an NVIDIA slide. The whitepaper (p. 13) confirms 1.3 pJ per bit for NVLink-C2C and a ratio above 5 to PCIe Gen 5. Horowitz (ISSCC 2014) supports the order of magnitude of DRAM access energy. The pJ per flop values are not confirmed by an opened source, and the slide does not state what they include.

The ABINIT segment heights (CPU-bound about 0.43; transfer about 0.40 and 0.04; CPU about 0.17) are read from a projected chart with an uncertainty of about 0.03; the speedups 1.16 and 4.25 are quoted from the slide, which the whitepaper (Figure 19, p. 30) calls a performance simulation.

Measurement conditions: one 32 GiB DDR4-3200 module (Windows CIM query, 2026-10-26), single channel, pin rate 25.6 GB/s; WSL 2 guest; hybrid processor; other agents' jobs shared the machine. Thread placement was not controlled. The guest shows no hardware performance counters (/sys/bus/event_source/devices lists only software events), so DRAM traffic per point was not measured: the 24 bytes per point are a model with write allocate. Printed timing tables are the best of five complete runs by a stated rule and are faster than typical runs; ranges over the five runs are given in the text.

Unexplained measurements: dependent loads from working sets of 4 and 8 MiB cost 96-158 ns although the guest reports a 12 MiB L3; kernels with stores reach 19.5-21.8 GB/s of assumed DRAM traffic while the read-only dot product of exercise 6 reaches 15.3-16.8 GB/s at 4 and 8 threads and the streaming-store triad 16.4 GB/s at 4 threads in the sample; the best of five Jacobi runs at 4 threads (4.92 Gflop/s) is 9 % above the roof computed from the scale kernel (4.53); twelve threads are slower than eight in all five runs of the sweep; the 12-thread FMA rate was 196-210 Gflop/s in the five kept runs and 233-290 Gflop/s in four earlier runs (thermal or power state suspected, not tested). The dot-product program of exercise 6 was run three times and is not a code-lab listing. The write-only fill (fill_mini.c) gives a streaming-over-ordinary ratio of 2.05-2.21 at 1 thread and 1.17-1.46 at 4 threads; at 4 threads the ordinary fill (14.6 GB/s asked for) would move 29.2 GB/s under full write allocate, above the 25.6 GB/s pin rate, so the 3/2 factor for the scale kernel is an upper estimate and the sweep's Q lies between 16 and 24 bytes per point.
Timestamps are section anchors from local speech-recognition segment times and locate topic changes to within a few seconds.

The machine transcript mishears technical words; all numbers and names in the chapter were taken from slide frames or from the sources, and no statement is attributed to the speech where the slide or a source gives the value.

lecture_corrections.claim: A read from storage costs a few thousand clock cycles (W3L3 9:59-10:30; repeated in context).
lecture_corrections.correction: The lecture's own slide gives 10 000 000 ns, which is 1e7 cycles at 1 GHz and 4e7 at 4 GHz.

lecture_corrections.claim: Ratios between memory levels are kept when technology improves (W3L3 14:20-14:52, in context).
lecture_corrections.correction: The statement concerns transfer rates. For latency it is contradicted: CPU +50 %/yr against DRAM +7 %/yr (Machanick 2002) gives a gap growing by 1.40 per year. For bandwidth, the ridge point grew by at most a factor of 3.8 between 2008 and the machines of Table 10.3.
lecture_corrections.evidence: Machanick 2002 Sec. 1; Williams et al. Sec. 6.3; Table 10.3

lecture_corrections.claim: CPU is SISD and GPU is SIMD (annotated on the slide, W3L4 7:21).
lecture_corrections.correction: CPUs execute SIMD (256-bit FMA measured); the GPU model is SIMT.
The slide shows the number of TOP500 systems with accelerators, 2006-2014, not the performance share.

lecture_corrections.claim: Slide: 70 Tflop/s FP64 for the Grace Hopper Superchip.
lecture_corrections.correction: Datasheet: 34 Tflop/s FP64 and 67 Tflop/s FP64 tensor core; 67 + 3.46 (Grace CPU) = 70.5 suggests the slide adds the two, which it does not say.

lecture_corrections.claim: Slide: Grace Hopper 4.25 times faster (bar chart).
lecture_corrections.correction: One application (ABINIT, 255-atom titanium) from a performance simulation.

lecture_corrections.claim: Slide: 36 Grace CPUs with NVLink, 130 TB/s.
lecture_corrections.correction: The slide shows GB200 NVL72: 36 Grace CPUs and 72 Blackwell GPUs; 130 TB/s is the NVLink bandwidth among the 72 GPUs.

lecture_corrections.claim: Frontier peak 1.7 Eflop/s (overview) and 2 Eflop/s (fun facts); 26.5 Tflop/s per GCD.
lecture_corrections.correction: Two bases for peak; OLCF guide gives 23.9 Tflop/s per GCD.
lecture_corrections.evidence: slides f0013, f0050 (W3L4); OLCF guide; TOP500

sections.section: The objects of the chapter and the running case
sections.lecture_material: Running problem of the book (Jacobi sweep) and the question of whether memory limits it.
sections.teaching_construction: Formal model of a program run (F, Q, I) and a machine (P_peak, B_peak, hierarchy); the bound T >= max(F/P, Q/B); machine description with the installed memory and its pin rate.

sections.section: The memory hierarchy: speed, size and the width of the paths
sections.lecture_material: Von Neumann cycle; pyramid of memory levels; speeds, sizes, costs; path widths 8 B, 32 B, 4 KB; bandwidths; warehouse analogy.
sections.teaching_construction: Correction of the cycle count; latency and bandwidth measurement by working-set size (hierarchy.c); half-performance length; bytes in flight.

sections.lecture_material: Virtual address space, pages, paging, thrashing, contiguous access.
sections.teaching_construction: Page, frame, page table, fault model; fault cost measurement (faults.c); average time with faults; the thrashing cliff table (amat.py).

sections.section: Hit time, miss penalty, the average access time and the memory wall
sections.lecture_material: Hit, miss, hit rate, miss rate, hit time, miss penalty; hierarchy numbers.
sections.research_extension: Wulf and McKee as reported by Machanick; Ertl critique.
sections.teaching_construction: AMAT and two-level AMAT; failure of AMAT for streaming; memory-wall extrapolation.

sections.section: STREAM: the bandwidth that the memory delivers
sections.research_extension: McCalpin STREAM rules and byte-counting conventions.
sections.teaching_construction: stream_mini.c with a streaming-store triad to test write allocate; interpretation.

sections.section: The Roofline model: derivation, assumptions and the ceilings of this machine
sections.teaching_construction: Derivation from (10.1); assumptions A1-A3; peak_fma.c; ridge points of the machine.

sections.section: The Jacobi sweep under the roof
sections.teaching_construction: Intensity of the sweep in three cache cases; layer condition; jacobi_bench.c, roofline.py, jacobi_check.c.

sections.section: Shared-memory and distributed-memory machines, and the node of a leadership system
sections.lecture_material: Shared versus distributed memory; MPPs; CPU versus GPU; Frontier node, GPU, network, programming environment, uses; Spacetime2.
sections.research_extension: OLCF user guide; HPE talk 2023; TOP500; Kim et al. dragonfly.
sections.teaching_construction: Multi-link bound (10.11); Frontier numbers check; bandwidth ladder; dragonfly port budget and cut capacity; halo ratio; capacity and power per flop.

sections.section: The Grace Hopper superchip and the economics of moving data
sections.lecture_material: Grand-challenge applications, ML/DL, digital twins, Moore, energy, Grace CPU, Hopper GPU, NVLink-C2C, energy per bit, co-scheduling, ABINIT.
sections.teaching_construction: Cost-error orders; ridge-point table; GH200 flop per byte and Jacobi bounds; energy per operand and per Jacobi point; ABINIT bar accounting.

symbol_ledger.definition: Flop count, DRAM bytes, arithmetic (operational) intensity.
Peak arithmetic rate, peak DRAM bandwidth, ridge point P_peak/B_peak. B_peak is a sustained rate measured with STREAM; B_pin (10.2) is the pin-rate limit.
Latency, bytes, bandwidth, half-performance length tau*B, bytes in flight tau*B.
Hit time, miss rate, miss penalty, average memory access time.
Memory time, fault service time, fault rate, array size in bytes, resident bytes.
Bytes over link k, intensity and bandwidth of link k.

symbol_ledger.symbol: nu, a, gamma, r, g, M
symbol_ledger.definition: Dragonfly (Kim et al. write p, a, h, k, g, N): terminals per router, routers per group, global channels per router, router radix, number of groups, number of terminals.
The scalar of the STREAM scale and triad kernels.
Tile edge and tiles of the blocked matrix multiplication of exercise 2.
Interior points per side, grid and its update, index macro (as Chapter 9).
Pin-rate limit of the memory module, transfers per second times bytes per transfer (10.2); upper limit of B_peak.
Fraction of a full write-allocate read that an ordinary store costs, 0 <= w <= 1; the sweep moves Q = 16 + 8w bytes per point.
Fraction of the bytes of a working set served by DRAM.
phi: fraction of the bandwidth B that a transfer reaches; b_phi: transfer size that reaches it, phi/(1-phi) * tau*B.
